EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT NOTE - 09/26/2023 (copy received by fax)

Chief complaint: right shoulder pain after a fall.

HPI: 70-year-old woman with osteoporosis and hypertension. Out for her usual morning walk, she went down, landing on her right hand with the arm straight out. Immediate severe pain in the right shoulder and she has not been able to move the arm since. Did not hit her head, no loss of consciousness, no neck pain. No dizziness or chest pain before the fall.

PMH: osteoporosis; hypertension; Graves disease, on methimazole; paroxysmal atrial fibrillation; bilateral knee osteoarthritis.
PSH: left cataract surgery.
Meds: hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily; methimazole 10 mg daily; calcium carbonate 600 mg three times daily; vitamin D3 2000 units daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: never smoker, social wine.

Exam: uncomfortable, holding right arm against her side. Right arm held adducted and appears shortened; acromion prominent with loss of the normal rounded contour of the shoulder. Reduced light-touch sensation over the lateral aspect of the right shoulder. Radial pulse 2+, hand warm, fingers move, sensation intact in the hand. Cervical spine nontender. No other injuries found on secondary survey.

Imaging: right shoulder films show the humeral head dislocated anteriorly and a fracture across the humeral surgical neck.
Labs: CBC, BMP and coagulation studies unremarkable.

Course: pain treated in the department, arm immobilized in a sling. Orthopedics consulted in the ED; given the fracture-dislocation, closed reduction was not attempted here. Plan for operative fixation.

Impression: right shoulder fracture-dislocation (anterior dislocation, humeral surgical neck fracture) after a ground-level fall - fragility fracture.
Disposition: admitted to orthopedics.

events.reason: Right proximal humerus fracture-dislocation, operative fixation

reports.text: Right shoulder, postoperative AP and scapular Y views. Interval open reduction and internal fixation of the proximal humerus with a lateral locking plate and screws. The glenohumeral joint is reduced. Fracture fragments in improved alignment. Screw tips do not breach the articular surface. Skin staples and soft tissue changes from surgery.
reports.conclusion: Postoperative ORIF right proximal humerus; glenohumeral joint reduced, hardware in expected position.

documents.title: Operative report - ORIF right proximal humerus
documents.author: orthopedics
documents.body:
OPERATIVE REPORT
Date of surgery: 09/27/2023
Preoperative / postoperative diagnosis: right anterior glenohumeral fracture-dislocation, surgical neck of humerus.
Procedure: open reduction of the glenohumeral dislocation; ORIF, right proximal humerus, locking plate.
Anesthesia: general with interscalene block.
Findings: humeral head dislocated anteriorly; displaced surgical neck fracture; poor bone quality consistent with osteoporosis.
Description: beach-chair position, deltopectoral approach. Humeral head reduced into the glenoid. Fracture reduced under fluoroscopy and fixed with a proximal humeral locking plate and screws. Stable through range of motion. Wound irrigated and closed in layers, staples to skin.
EBL minimal. No complications. Neurovascular status in the hand intact at the end of the case.
Plan: sling, pendulum exercises after the first week, outpatient physical therapy, clinic in 2 weeks for staple removal.

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary - orthopedics

DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted: 09/26/2023 via ED. Discharged: 09/29/2023.
Diagnosis: right shoulder anterior dislocation with humeral surgical neck fracture (fragility fracture). Osteoporosis.
Procedure: ORIF right proximal humerus, 09/27/2023.

Course: taken to the OR on hospital day 2 for open reduction and plate fixation, uncomplicated. Postoperative films with the joint reduced and hardware in good position. Pain well controlled by discharge. Mobilizing independently on the ward; cleared by physical therapy for home. The patch of reduced sensation over the lateral shoulder noted in the ED was still present at discharge; to be rechecked in clinic.
Hemoglobin stable after surgery.

Discharge medications: unchanged home medications - hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, methimazole 10 mg daily, calcium carbonate 600 mg TID, vitamin D3 2000 units daily.
Allergies: NKDA.

Instructions: sling at all times except for hygiene and pendulum exercises; no lifting with the right arm; keep incision dry until staple removal. Outpatient physical therapy referral placed. Orthopedic clinic in about 2 weeks. Follow up with primary care within 1 week.

documents.title: Endocrinology follow-up letter
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Dear colleague,

Ms. Walsh came in on 11/10/2023 for routine follow-up, this time with questions of her own about her bones. Osteoporosis was found on her first DXA in July 2021, and in September she fractured the right humeral surgical neck (with an anterior dislocation) in a fall from standing, fixed surgically on 9/27. She wanted to understand what the fracture says about her bones and whether she should change how she eats.

Since the fracture she has deliberately added dairy and more green vegetables; despite her lactose intolerance she is tolerating the amounts she takes. She lives on her own and walks every day. She has no back pain, no joint pain and no difficulty walking. Nothing in her history suggests a malignancy, malabsorption or other chronic illness. Menopause at 45, never on hormone therapy. Screening is current: the 2016 colonoscopy and her most recent mammogram were both clear.

Medications: methimazole 10 mg daily; hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily; calcium carbonate 600 mg three times daily; vitamin D3 2000 units daily.
Allergies: none known.
Family history: mother with an osteoporotic hip fracture at 82; sister with Graves disease. No family history of kidney stones.

Exam: vital signs normal. Thin, well-appearing woman. Spine without tenderness or deformity. Gait steady. Neurological examination normal. Thyroid not enlarged.

DXA 10/24/2023: L1-L4 T-score -2.7, left femoral neck -2.9.
Labs today: calcium, creatinine, albumin, alkaline phosphatase, liver enzymes, TSH, free T4 and 25-hydroxyvitamin D all within normal limits. No secondary cause of bone loss is evident, and none of these results was expected to be abnormal in her case.

Assessment: postmenopausal osteoporosis with a fragility fracture; Graves disease, euthyroid on methimazole 10 mg.
Discussion: I explained that a fracture after a fall from standing, together with her T-scores, puts her at high risk of another fracture over the next few years, and that the hip number has slipped since 2021. We reviewed the treatment choices again - an oral or intravenous bisphosphonate, denosumab, and the bone-building injectables. She listened carefully and decided against any bone medication for now; she remains worried about side effects. Dairy in the amounts she is having is fine and gives her calcium from food. Continue calcium carbonate and vitamin D3, weight-bearing activity and fall precautions.
Plan: continue methimazole 10 mg; TSH/free T4 every 6 months at your lab; see her again in a year.

Endocrinology

Admission 07/07/2024 - Discharge 07/10/2024

- hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily
- methimazole 10 mg daily

events.reason: Painful skin lesions, abdomen and thighs

documents.title: Emergency Department provider note
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT NOTE - 07/13/2024

Chief complaint: burning skin pain and dark patches on the lower abdomen and thighs.

HPI: 71-year-old woman discharged from this hospital three days ago after a short admission for atrial fibrillation, started on warfarin 5 mg daily on 7/8. Yesterday she developed burning pain in the skin of the lower abdomen and upper thighs, and the areas have darkened and spread quickly since. No fever. No trauma, no injections or procedures to these sites. She has never had a blood clotting problem and knows of no clotting disorder in her family.

PMH: paroxysmal atrial fibrillation; hypertension; Graves disease; osteoporosis with right proximal humerus fracture (ORIF 2023); knee osteoarthritis.
Meds: warfarin 5 mg daily (started 7/8); hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg; methimazole 10 mg; calcium carbonate 600 mg TID; vitamin D3 2000 units.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: vital signs stable, afebrile. Several sharply bordered violaceous plaques across the lower abdomen and the tops of both thighs, some with overlying bullae and areas of frank necrosis. Exquisitely tender. No surrounding cellulitis, no warmth or drainage, no crepitus. No bleeding from any site, no bruising elsewhere. Peripheral pulses present and equal bilaterally.

Labs: platelets normal; hemoglobin stable compared with discharge; INR 3.2; fibrinogen 150 mg/dL (ref 200-400).

Assessment: warfarin-induced skin necrosis, onset on day 5-6 of warfarin; hypofibrinogenemia. No evidence of infection.
Plan: warfarin stopped. Vitamin K. Heparin infusion for anticoagulation. Wound care consult. Admit to medicine.

documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL - DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admission 07/13/2024 - Discharge 07/17/2024
Principal diagnosis: warfarin-induced skin necrosis.
Secondary: hypofibrinogenemia (fibrinogen 150 mg/dL on admission); paroxysmal atrial fibrillation; hypertension; Graves disease; osteoporosis.

Course: presented three days after discharge with painful necrotic plaques of the lower abdomen and upper thighs, INR 3.2, six days after warfarin was started. Warfarin was stopped in the ED. She received vitamin K 5 mg IV and was started on an unfractionated heparin infusion. INR back to normal the next morning. Wound care nursing saw her daily: lesions cleaned, bullae left intact, nonadherent dressings. No new lesions after admission and no signs of infection. Platelet count and hemoglobin stayed stable throughout. Remained in sinus rhythm.
At discharge the heparin infusion was changed to enoxaparin, 1 mg/kg (55 kg) every 12 hours; first dose given before she left and injection teaching completed.

Discharge medications:
- NEW enoxaparin 55 mg subcutaneously every 12 hours
- STOPPED warfarin
- hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily
- methimazole 10 mg daily
- calcium carbonate 600 mg three times daily
- vitamin D3 2000 units daily
Allergies: NKDA.

Follow-up: PCP within one week for wound check; dressing changes every few days (supplies sent home). Long-term anticoagulation plan to be decided with cardiology once the skin has healed.

documents.body:

Dressings changed this morning, no pus or fever.
Monday's INR draw was cancelled (no longer on warfarin). Keeping PCP visit 7/22. Asked her to bring her dressing supplies.

documents.title: Post-Hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
TCM visit after two admissions this month. Both discharge summaries and the ED note reviewed.
- 7/7-7/10: AF (second episode; first was the thyrotoxic AF in 2021). Euthyroid. Converted on her own. Warfarin 5 mg started 7/8.
- 7/13-7/17: warfarin skin necrosis of lower abdomen and thighs, INR 3.2, fibrinogen 150. Warfarin stopped; vitamin K, heparin drip, wound care. Discharged on enoxaparin 55 mg q12h.

Today: skin much less painful. No fever. Injections going OK, a few small bruises at injection sites. No other bleeding. No palpitations.
Meds: enoxaparin 55 mg SC q12h; HCTZ 25; methimazole 10; calcium carbonate 600 TID; D3 2000. Warfarin stopped.

Exam: vitals per flowsheet. Lower abdomen and both upper thighs: the lesions are crusting over, with dry eschar centrally and pink margins; no surrounding erythema, warmth, drainage or odor. No new lesions. Heart RRR. Lungs clear.
CBC today normal (resulted this afternoon) - platelets fine on enoxaparin.

A/P:
1. Warfarin skin necrosis, healing, no infection. Dressing changes here by our nurse twice weekly to start, then weekly; she does in-between changes at home.
2. Paroxysmal AF, in sinus. On enoxaparin for now. Referral to cardiology's anticoagulation clinic for the long-term plan once healed.
3. Hypofibrinogenemia noted during admission.
4. HTN, Graves, osteoporosis - unchanged.

documents.title: Anticoagulation clinic - warfarin restart
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
CARDIOLOGY ANTICOAGULATION CLINIC - 08/26/2024

Referred for anticoagulation in paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (episodes 2021 while thyrotoxic, and 7/2024 while euthyroid). Warfarin 5 mg was started 7/8 and stopped 7/13 for skin necrosis with hypofibrinogenemia; she has been on enoxaparin 55 mg every 12 hours since 7/17.
Skin lesions now fully healed (PCP nurse 8/20). No bleeding. In sinus rhythm by exam.
Baseline labs 8/22 at her PCP's lab: liver and renal function normal, CBC normal.

Plan:
- Restart warfarin 5 mg daily this evening, with enoxaparin 55 mg q12h continued as cover.
- INR on day 2 (8/27), day 4 (8/29) and day 5 (8/30) at her PCP's lab. Enoxaparin stops once INR is 2.0 or above.
- INR goal 2.0-3.0.
- Report any new painful skin discoloration at once.
- Warfarin education reviewed: consistent vitamin K intake, alcohol, checking before any new prescription, OTC or supplement.
Cardiology clinic visit 9/11.

documents.title: Annual Wellness Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
AWV 2024.

A hard year medically: AF admission in July, then warfarin skin necrosis and a second admission; skin healed by 8/20; warfarin restarted 8/26 by the anticoagulation clinic, enoxaparin stopped 8/30 with INR in her goal range.

Fall screen: POSITIVE - fall with fracture 9/26/2023, just under 12 months ago. No falls since. Wears shoes with better grip. TUG normal today. Not fearful of falling but more careful.
PHQ-2: 1 - says the summer wore her down; enjoying things again now. Not depressed.
Cognition: no concerns.
Function: independent in ADLs/IADLs.
Diet: eats as before - dairy most days, greens most days, consistent. Calcium carbonate 600 TID and D3 unchanged. No other supplements.
Alcohol: rare glass of wine; we talked about keeping it light and steady on warfarin.

Meds: warfarin 5 mg daily (anticoag clinic doses); HCTZ 25 daily; methimazole 10 daily; calcium carbonate 600 TID; D3 2000 daily.

Exam: vitals per flowsheet. RRR. Lungs clear. Skin: healed lesions lower abdomen/thighs with residual pigment.

Plan:
- Warfarin counselling reinforced: same diet week to week, tell us or the clinic before any new prescription, antibiotic, OTC pain reliever or supplement; no NSAIDs.
- BMP today.
- Mammogram due 11/2024 - order placed.
- Vaccines: flu and COVID in October.
- Fall prevention reviewed; consider home safety check of stairs.
- Cardiology visit tomorrow.

documents.title: Cardiology follow-up letter
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Dear colleague,

I saw Ms. Walsh, 71, on 09/11/2024 to follow her anticoagulation for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Her course this summer included hypofibrinogenemia found with warfarin skin necrosis in July. Warfarin was restarted 8/26 at 5 mg under enoxaparin cover.

She is taking warfarin exactly as instructed. She has felt well, eats the way she did before, and has not started anything new over the counter - her calcium carbonate and vitamin D are the same as always. No bleeding, no bruising beyond the old injection marks, no new skin changes, no symptoms of clots.

Medications: warfarin 5 mg daily; hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily; methimazole 10 mg daily; calcium carbonate 600 mg TID; vitamin D3 2000 units daily.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: vital signs as recorded, regular rhythm, no murmur, lungs clear, no edema. Healed skin areas without new lesions.

Data: baseline labs before the restart, including liver and renal function, were normal. INR 1.1 on day 2 and 2.2 on day 4 of the restart, then 2.4 on day 5, when enoxaparin was stopped. I explained to her that warfarin takes several days to bring the INR into range, which is why the injections overlapped.

Assessment: long-term anticoagulant therapy with warfarin for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation; clinically stable, no bleeding or thrombosis.
Plan: continue warfarin 5 mg daily, INR goal 2-3, INRs at her PCP's lab with dosing by our anticoagulation clinic. See her in a year.

Cardiology

documents.body:
Dear colleague,

Annual follow-up for Sandra Walsh on 11/14/2024. Graves disease, euthyroid on methimazole 10 mg daily. TSH and free T4 normal today, as they were in March and at her July admission.
She had a difficult summer (AF admission, then warfarin skin necrosis); now back on warfarin through cardiology's clinic. Her AF episode in July occurred while euthyroid.
No hyperthyroid symptoms. Thyroid not enlarged. Osteoporosis: still declines medication; on calcium carbonate 600 mg TID and vitamin D3 2000 units.
Plan: continue methimazole 10 mg. TSH/free T4 every 6 months at your lab. Return in one year.

Endocrinology
